title: Meditation as practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth perfection: effort, tuned like a lute string, neither too tight nor too loose.

A man has been starving himself in the forest for a long time. In the story, he eats so little that when he touches his belly he can feel his spine. He holds his breath until there's a roaring in his ears. Nothing he's looking for comes. Then, worn down to almost nothing, he remembers an afternoon from when he was a small boy. His father was at work in the fields. The boy sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind went quiet and glad all by itself. The man is the future Buddha, and you met that tree early on the path. The memory changes his whole path. Today, the fifth perfection: meditation.
screen: `STARVING HIMSELF IN THE FOREST.` → `A BOY UNDER A ROSE-APPLE TREE.` → `THE MEMORY THAT CHANGED THE PATH.`

segments.voice: In the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha tells this himself. Remembering the rose-apple tree, he asks: could that be the way to awakening? And he answers: that is the way. Then he asks why he should be afraid of a happiness that has nothing to do with sense pleasures or unwholesome things. He decides not to be afraid of it. He eats a little rice, gets his strength back, and sits. So meditation here doesn't start with force. It starts with a calm he already knew, and a willingness to trust it. The Pali word for those deep absorptions is jhana. In Sanskrit it's dhyana, and in the Mahayana list of perfections dhyana is the fifth: meditative steadiness, a mind that can stay. Tradition says the name of the Chan school in China, Zen in Japan, comes from this same word. The second side is steady, daily. At the close of one teaching in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha puts it plainly. Here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't be careless, or you'll regret it later. He points at an ordinary place and says, sit there. The perfection isn't one great sitting. It's the habit of sitting, the way a path through a field is made by walking it every day. A long sitting now and then is good. A short one every day wears the path in.
screen: `THE MEMORY OF THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` · `NO NEED TO FEAR THAT CALM.` · `DHYANA, THE FIFTH PERFECTION.` · then, large: `THE ROOTS OF TREES: SIT THERE.`

segments.voice: Find your own patch of shade: sit easy and upright, hands resting, and let the breath come and go without managing it. When the mind wanders, and it will, notice where it went and come back, the way the Buddha came back to a quiet afternoon. No need to force anything.
Meditation as practice. Dhyana, the fifth perfection: a steady mind, built by sitting a little every day. Today's word.
Your line: the fifth perfection. A bench, a parked car or a quiet stair can be the root of a tree. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists in many schools keep a daily sitting practice at home or in a temple, often at the same time each day; in the Mahayana list of six perfections, meditation (dhyana) is the fifth.

original.note: Sanskrit dhyana (Pali jhana): meditative absorption; the fifth of the six perfections in the Mahayana list.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means forcing your mind to go blank.
what it means: dhyana, a steady, settled mind, trusted rather than forced, and built by sitting daily.
what a scholar hears: the rose-apple memory in the Middle Length Discourses, and the line 'here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts' at the close of the Discourse on Two Kinds of Thought.

chat.says: How did the Buddha finally find his way into meditation?
options: He remembered a calm he'd felt as a boy under a tree, and trusted it.
He fasted and held his breath harder than ever, until it broke open.
A teacher handed him a secret technique on the night he woke up.
chat.meaning: In the Middle Length Discourses he recalls the rose-apple tree, decides not to fear that calm, eats, and sits: it begins with trust, not force.

rose-apple tree.meaning: the tree whose shade held the boy's quiet, glad calm

jhana.meaning: a deep meditative absorption, in Pali

dhyana.meaning: Sanskrit for meditation; the fifth perfection

Chan.meaning: the Chinese meditation school, called Zen in Japan

Middle Length Discourses.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's discourses in Pali

notes: MN 36 paraphrased: extreme fasting (feeling the spine through the belly), breathless meditation with roaring in the head, the rose-apple memory while his father (the Sakyan) was working, 'that is the path to awakening', not fearing pleasure apart from sensuality, taking solid food. Confirm the order and wording; 'years' of austerities is not stated in MN 36 itself and could be softened.
'The roots of trees, empty huts; meditate, do not be negligent, lest you regret it later' paraphrased from MN 19 and other closing passages; confirm citation.
Chan/Zen name derived from dhyana framed as 'tradition says'; it is standard but is an etymology claim. Confirm or cut.
Index practice is 'sit twenty minutes'; the app sit is two minutes, so the practice invites scheduling a twenty-minute sit later.
